thesis: Whether vice and virtue are real distinctions (Franklin's 1725 Dissertation argues from God's omnipotence and goodness that nothing is really evil and 'vice and virtue are empty distinctions'; the Autobiography calls the pamphlet an erratum and holds that actions are bad because they harm us).

early.text: Tho' a Creature may do many Actions which by his Fellow Creatures will be nam'd Evil, and which will naturally and necessarily cause or bring upon the Doer, certain Pains (which will likewise be call'd Punishments;) yet this Proposition proves, that he cannot act what will be in itself really Ill, or displeasing to God. And that the painful Consequences of his evil Actions (so call'd) are not, as indeed they ought not to be, Punishments or Unhappinesses, will be shewn hereafter.
early.work: A Dissertation on Liberty and Necessity, Pleasure and Pain (1725 pamphlet)
early.locator: Sect. I, comment after Prop. VI

announced.text: and from the attributes of God, his infinite wisdom, goodness and power, concluded that nothing could possibly be wrong in the world, and that vice and virtue were empty distinctions, no such things existing, appear'd now not so clever a performance as I once thought it; and I doubted whether some error had not insinuated itself unperceiv'd into my argument, so as to infect all that follow'd, as is common in metaphysical reasonings.
announced.work: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Part One, written 1771; Harvard Classics 1909 text, from the Bigelow edition)
announced.locator: Part One, the London episode, paragraph after the Dryden motto ('My London pamphlet ... appear'd now not so clever a performance')

unannounced.text: Revelation had indeed no weight with me, as such; but I entertain'd an opinion that, though certain actions might not be bad because they were forbidden by it, or good because it commanded them, yet probably these actions might be forbidden because they were bad for us, or commanded because they were beneficial to us, in their own natures, all the circumstances of things considered.
unannounced.work: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Part One, written 1771; Harvard Classics 1909 text, from the Bigelow edition)
unannounced.locator: Part One, paragraph after 'I grew convinc'd that truth, sincerity and integrity'

control.text: I might here observe, how necessary a Thing in the Order and Design of the Universe this Pain or Uneasiness is, and how beautiful in its Place! Let us but suppose it just now banish'd the World entirely, and consider the Consequence of it: All the Animal Creation would immediately stand stock still, exactly in the Posture they were in the Moment Uneasiness departed; not a Limb, not a Finger would henceforth move; we should all be reduc'd to the Condition of Statues, dull and unactive: Here I should continue to sit motionless with the Pen in my Hand thus ------ and neither leave my Seat nor write one Letter more.
control.work: A Dissertation on Liberty and Necessity, Pleasure and Pain (1725 pamphlet)
control.locator: Sect. II, comment after Prop. II

notes: Early work: Wikisource has the 1725 text; I saved its plain-text extract (MediaWiki API prop=extracts, saved as diss_ex.json, sha256 below) and rewrote it with a blank line between paragraphs as diss.txt (the file used here), so the paragraph splitter works; words are unchanged. Wikisource labels it PD-old. Later work: Gutenberg #148, the 1909 Harvard Classics reprint of the Bigelow text; Part One was written in 1771 (the text opens 'Twyford ... 1771'); first printed 1791 in French, so year=1791. The announced passage is the sentence after the Dryden verse and starts mid-sentence ('and from the attributes of God'); it retracts ('appear'd now not so clever a performance as I once thought it; and I doubted whether some error had not insinuated itself') but does not itself state the new view, which comes in the next paragraph ('I grew convinc'd that truth, sincerity and integrity ... were of the utmost importance'); the unannounced passage (actions 'might be forbidden because they were bad for us') states it without any change language, though it sits a few paragraphs after the announcement. Franklin also says 'My printing this pamphlet was another erratum' a few lines earlier. Wikipedia: Franklin 'acknowledges how offensive this idea would be to the reader, and refuted it later.' diss_ex.json sha256=a0dc8d60d39c90fffa9e30d9a909b64ea9ff7cf07faf5d434309510318842fd2.

thesis: Whether reason and the evidence of nature give any support to theism (the anonymous 1878 Candid Examination finds no evidence and rests on pure syllogistic reasoning; Romanes's own 1890s Notes say that treatise made two 'wellnigh fatal oversights' and that the religious consciousness of human nature is evidence).

early.text: Having fully demonstrated that there is no shadow of a positive argument in support of the theistic theory, there arose the danger that some persons might erroneously conclude that for this reason the theistic theory must be untrue. It therefore became necessary to point out, that although, as far as we can see, nature does not require an Intelligent Cause to account for any of her phenomena, yet it is possible that, if we could see farther, we should see that nature could not be what she is unless she had owed her existence to an Intelligent Cause.
early.work: A Candid Examination of Theism, by 'Physicus' (1878)
early.locator: Chapter VII (General Summary and Conclusions), Sec. 48

announced.text: But I now clearly perceive two wellnigh fatal oversights which I then committed. The first was undue confidence in merely syllogistic conclusions, even when derived from sound premises, in regions of such high abstraction. The second was, in not being sufficiently careful in examining the foundations of my criticism, i. e. the validity of its premises.
announced.work: Thoughts on Religion (1895), Romanes's own 'Notes for a work on A Candid Examination of Religion' (editor's introduction and concluding note excluded)

unannounced.text: Therefore it is as absurd to say that the religious consciousness of minds other than our own can be barred antecedently as evidence, as it is to say that testimony to the miraculous is similarly barred.
unannounced.work: Thoughts on Religion (1895), Romanes's own 'Notes for a work on A Candid Examination of Religion' (editor's introduction and concluding note excluded)
unannounced.locator: Notes, section on evidence from the religious consciousness, p. 150

control.text: How far the great principle of natural selection may have been instrumental in the evolution of organic forms, is not here, as Mill erroneously imagined, the question; the question is simply as to whether we are to accept the theory of special creation or the theory of organic evolution. And forasmuch as no competent judge at the present time can hesitate for one moment in answering this question, the argument from a proximate teleology must be regarded as no longer having any rational existence.
control.work: A Candid Examination of Theism, by 'Physicus' (1878)
control.locator: Chapter VII, Sec. 48 (argument from design / evolution)

notes: Early work is Gutenberg #19003 (clean text). Later work is the archive.org OCR djvu text of Thoughts on Religion (1895, posthumous; ed. Charles Gore): OCR leaves double spaces, page headers ('A Candid Examination of Religion 101') and hyphenation artifacts, which I avoided in the chosen passages (the announced passage lies inside one printed page, p. 101). The span is Romanes's own Notes only (from 'NOTES FOR A WORK ON A CANDID EXAMINATION OF RELIGION' to the line before the editor's 'Concluding Note'), but it contains Gore's bracketed '[... -- ED.]' footnotes. Dates: the Candid Examination was written by 1876 and published 1878; the Notes are from c. 1890-94 (one note dated 1893; Romanes died 1894), so written=1893 is an estimate. The announced passage is a retraction of method ('undue confidence in merely syllogistic conclusions'; careless foundations) and does not itself state the new view; the surrounding page says 'the negative conclusions reached in the former essay have been greatly modified by the results of maturer thought'. Note the early passage already hedges ('it is possible that, if we could see farther ...'), so the conflict is one of confidence and weight. Wikipedia: 'A Candid Examination of Theism, where he concluded that God's existence was not supported by the evidence' and 'Towards the end of his life, he returned to Christianity.'

thesis: Whether private and domestic attachments may override impartial justice (Political Justice: 'what magic is there in the pronoun my'; the 1799 St. Leon preface says he wishes to modify the earlier chapters because domestic and private affections are inseparable from human nature and compatible with justice).

early.text: This would not alter the truth of the proposition. The life of Fenelon would still be more valuable than that of the valet ; and justice, pure, unadulterated justice, would still have preferred that which was most valuable. Justice would have taught me to save the life of Fenelon at the expense of the other. What magic is there in the pronoun " my," that should justify us in overturning the decisions of impartial truth ?
early.work: Enquiry Concerning Political Justice (first ed. 1793; text from the 4th ed., 1843, vol. 1, reprinting the 1798 3rd-ed. text)
early.locator: Book II, Chap. II 'Of Justice' (the Fenelon and the valet example)

announced.text: In answer to this objection, all I think it necessary to say on the present occasion is, that, for more than four years, I have been anxious for opportunity and leisure to modify some of the earlier chapters of that work in conformity to the sentiments inculcated in this. Not that I see cause to make any change respecting the principle of justice, or any thing else fundamental to the system there delivered; but that I apprehend domestic and private affections inseparable from the nature of man, and from what may be styled the culture of the heart, and am fully persuaded that they are not incompatible with a profound and active sense of justice in the mind of him that cherishes them.
announced.work: St. Leon: A Tale of the Sixteenth Century (1799; text from the 1831 Standard Novels edition), original Preface dated Nov. 26, 1799 and the novel
announced.locator: Original Preface, last two paragraphs (dated Nov. 26, 1799)

unannounced.text: To feel that we are loved by one whose love we have deserved, to be employed in the mutual interchange of the marks of this love, habitually to study the happiness of one by whom our happiness is studied in return, this is the most desirable, as it is the genuine and unadulterated condition of human nature. I must have some one to sympathise with; I cannot bear to be cut off from all relations: I desire to experience a confidence, a concord, an attachment, that cannot rise between common acquaintance.
unannounced.work: St. Leon: A Tale of the Sixteenth Century (1799; text from the 1831 Standard Novels edition), original Preface dated Nov. 26, 1799 and the novel
unannounced.locator: St. Leon's narration of domestic life, Vol. 1 (the 'I must have some one to sympathise with' passage)

control.text: If truth therefore can be brought home to the conviction of the individual, let us see how it stands with the public or the world. Now in the first place, it is extremely clear that, if no individual can resist the force of truth, it can be only necessary to apply this proposition from individual to individual, and, we shall at length comprehend the whole. Thus the affirmation in its literal sense is completely established.
control.work: Enquiry Concerning Political Justice (first ed. 1793; text from the 4th ed., 1843, vol. 1, reprinting the 1798 3rd-ed. text)
control.locator: Book I, Chap. V (running head 'Voluntary actions of men originate in their opinions'), p. 42, on the force of truth

notes: Early text: archive.org OCR djvu of the 1843 'fourth edition' of Political Justice vol. 1 (University of Toronto copy; it reprints the 1798 third-edition text, which says 'valet' where the 1793 first edition says 'chambermaid'). I checked the 1793 first edition (archive.org OCR of vol. 1, long s): the same argument stands there but in different words (1793: 'What magic is there in the pronoun "my," to overturn the decisions of everlasting truth? My wife or my mother may be a fool or a prostitute'; the 1798 text used here says 'that should justify us in overturning the decisions of impartial truth'), so the quoted wording is the 1798 revision, not the 1793 original. OCR leaves double spaces and spaced punctuation ('" my,"', 'truth ?') which are verbatim in the file. The early work is a 1793 book (written 1791-93); the text used is the 1798 revision, only one year before the preface, though the doctrine (private attachment may not override impartial justice) is the 1793 one and the early/announced gap by written date is 6 years. The announced passage is Godwin's own preface and states the new view ('I apprehend domestic and private affections inseparable from the nature of man'), while also saying he sees no change needed in the principle of justice, so the shift is one of partial revision. Gutenberg #53707 is the 1831 text; the 1799 preface is reproduced in it after a 1831 Advertisement. The unannounced passage is the narrator St. Leon's voice in a novel, which the preface says inculcates the new sentiments; the control (truth's force, a doctrine Godwin kept as 'fundamental') comes from Political Justice. SEP (Godwin): 'Thoughts Occasioned by ... Dr. Parr's Spital Sermon (1801) ... sought ... to confess errors which he now recognized--and which had already been acknowledged both in the revisions to the later editions of his Enquiry, and in his comments in St. Leon'; SEP also names the 'famous fire cause' (Fenelon and the valet) as Godwin's impartiality example.

thesis: Whether many minds or mental states can compound into a single higher consciousness, and hence whether a compound 'absolute' mind is possible (the Principles of Psychology denies it and calls the mind-dust theory untenable; A Pluralistic Universe says the absolute is not the impossible being he once thought).

early.text: We talk of the 'spirit of the age,' and the 'sentiment of the people,' and in various ways we hypostatize 'public opinion.' But we know this to be symbolic speech, and never dream that the spirit, opinion, sentiment, etc., constitute a consciousness other than, and additional to, that of the several individuals whom the words 'age,' 'people,' or 'public' denote. The private minds do not agglomerate into a higher compound mind.
early.work: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 1 (1890), Chapter VI 'The Mind-Stuff Theory'
early.locator: Chapter VI, section 'Some alleged proofs that mind-dust exists' (after the 'sentence of a dozen words' example)

announced.text: The absolute is not the impossible being I once thought it. Mental facts do function both singly and together, at once, and we finite minds may simultaneously be co-conscious with one another in a superhuman intelligence.
announced.work: A Pluralistic Universe (1909; Hibbert Lectures delivered 1908), Lecture V
announced.locator: Lecture VII 'The Continuity of Experience', end of the section on the intellectualist impasse (paragraph beginning 'We have now reached a point of view')

unannounced.text: In _principle_, then, the real units of our immediately-felt life are unlike the units that intellectualist logic holds to and makes its calculations with. They are not separate from their own others, and you have to take them at widely separated dates to find any two of them that seem unblent. Then indeed they do appear separate even as their concepts are separate; a chasm yawns between them; but the chasm itself is but an intellectualist fiction, got by abstracting from the continuous sheet of experiences with which the intermediary time was filled.
unannounced.work: A Pluralistic Universe (1909; Hibbert Lectures delivered 1908), Lecture V
unannounced.locator: Lecture VII, paragraph after 'our old objection to the self-compounding of states of consciousness ... is unfounded in principle'

control.text: Habit is thus the enormous fly-wheel of society, its most precious conservative agent. It alone is what keeps us all within the bounds of ordinance, and saves the children of fortune from the envious uprisings of the poor. It alone prevents the hardest and most repulsive walks of life from being deserted by those brought up to tread therein.
control.work: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 1 (1890), Chapter VI 'The Mind-Stuff Theory'

notes: Both Gutenberg texts are clean (Gutenberg #57628 vol. 1 of the Principles, #11984 A Pluralistic Universe). Italic markers appear as underscores (_belonging_, _principle_), which is verbatim. The span for the Principles starts at the body of Chapter I (the preface and contents are skipped) and runs to the end of vol. 1 including James's chapter footnotes; the span for the lectures runs from Lecture I to the line before the Index (appendices are James's own). The announced passage states the new view ('Mental facts do function both singly and together, at once, and we finite minds may simultaneously be co-conscious ...'); Lecture V of the same book narrates the earlier view as a 'direct personal confession' ('In the year 1890 I published a work on psychology ...', 'I found myself compelled, therefore, to call the absolute impossible'). The unannounced passage is in Lecture VII, the paragraph right after one that mentions 'our old objection', but its own sentences carry no change language. SEP Panpsychism: James 'advanced a cogent set of objections against ... the mind dust theory, in chapter six of The Principles of Psychology ([1890] 1981) ... But in the end James's commitment [to panpsychism] is quite clear (see James 1909, 1911 ...)'.

thesis: Whether hysteria is caused by actual sexual seduction or abuse in early childhood (the 1896 paper asserts that at the bottom of every case lie real premature sexual experiences; the 1905 paper says he overestimated their frequency and had mistaken the patients' phantasies for memories).

early.text: I put forward the proposition, therefore, that at the bottom of every case of hysteria will be found one or more experiences of premature sexual experience, belonging to the first years of childhood, experiences which may be reproduced by analytic work though whole decades have intervened. I believe this to be a momentous revelation, the discovery of a _caput Nili_ of neuropathology, but I hardly know from what point to continue the discussion of the situation.
early.work: The Aetiology of Hysteria (1896), in Collected Papers vol. I (1924, transl. under Joan Riviere), paper X
early.locator: Paper X, the section on the infantile scenes (after the scenes of puberty)

announced.text: I overestimated the frequency of these occurrences, which are otherwise quite authentic, and all the more so since I was not at this period able to discriminate between the deceptive memories of hysterics concerning their childhood and the memory-traces of actual happenings. I have since learned to unravel many a phantasy of seduction and found it to be an attempt at defence against the memory of sexual activities practised by the child himself (masturbation of children).
announced.work: My Views on the Part Played by Sexuality in the Aetiology of the Neuroses (1905), in Collected Papers vol. I (1924), paper XIV
announced.locator: Paper XIV, the paragraph 'It happened by chance that my earlier, not very plentiful material ...'

control.text: The value of what we discover in this way is, of course, impaired by all the various circumstances which commonly conceal from a patient the knowledge of his own condition---his lack of scientific understanding of ætiological influences, the fallacy _post hoc_, _ergo propter hoc_, the distress it causes him to think or speak of certain noxiæ and traumas. Hence, in making any such enquiry we adhere to the principle of not adopting the patients' belief without a thorough critical examination and not allowing them to lay down for us our scientific opinion upon the ætiology of the neurosis.
control.work: The Aetiology of Hysteria (1896), in Collected Papers vol. I (1924, transl. under Joan Riviere), paper X
control.locator: Paper X, opening paragraph (method of anamnestic enquiry)

notes: Early and later works are two separate papers (1896 and 1905) printed in the same Gutenberg volume (#79856, Collected Papers vol. I, International Psycho-Analytical Library no. 7, 1924, public domain), so both spans point at the same file with different line ranges (paper X; paper XIV). Gutenberg lists the release date as 2026; the book's original publication is 1924. The text keeps the book's {page} markers, which the chosen passages avoid. No unannounced passage: every statement of the new view in the 1905 paper (and in the 1914 History paper) is framed as a correction of the earlier theory. The announced passage states the new view (seduction 'phantasy' as defence against memories of the child's own sexual activity). Freud abandoned the theory privately in 1897 (letter to Fliess, 21 Sept 1897) and first said so publicly in 1905/06. Wikipedia (Seduction theory): 'Freud initially thought that his patients were relating more or less factual stories of sexual mistreatment ... Within a few years Freud abandoned his theory, concluding that some of his patients' stories of sexual abuse were not literal and were instead fantasies' and he 'did not make known his abandonment of the theory publicly until 1906'. The subject matter (child sexual abuse) is discussed clinically in the passages.

thesis: Whether the State should maintain an established church (in particular the Church of Ireland) as the vehicle of religious truth (Gladstone's 1838 book says governments are bound to maintain and propagate religious truth; his 1868 Chapter of Autobiography says he now thinks maintaining the Irish Establishment grossly unjust).

early.text: None of these writers regarded the subject in the aspect most imperatively required by present circumstances : namely, that which shows that governments are, by " dutiful necessity," cognizant of religious truth and falsehood, and bound to the maintenance and propagation of the former.
early.work: The State in Its Relations with the Church (1838; 3rd ed., 1839 text)

announced.text: My opinion of the Established Church of Ireland now is the direct opposite of what it was then. I then thought it reconcilable with civil and national justice; I now think the maintenance of it grossly unjust. I then thought its action was favourable to the interests of the religion which it teaches; I now believe it to be opposed to them.
announced.locator: Main text, after the summary of the book's propositions ('What I have now to show is the manner in which I retreated')

unannounced.text: I think we ought now to perceive that the annexation of the warrant of civil authority to the religious embassy of the Irish Church, discredits in lieu of recommending it in the view of the Irish people. I do not mean that we are to put down the Establishment for the sake of a more effective propagandism. We must not for a moment forget that civil justice, an adaptation of the state of things in Ireland to the essential principles of political right, is that one broad and more than sufficient justification of the measure, in which all its advocates agree.
unannounced.locator: Main text, paragraph on the West of Ireland missionary operations

control.text: The first assertion, then, of religious liberty was for the nation, as against what lay beyond the nation, and not for the private individual as against all but himself. And the doctrine grew imperceptibly by unconscious and progressive deflections from the rule of arbitrary power. But, however it be true that the doctrine of private judgment was not matured in a single day or by a single effort, it remains strictly and demonstrably true, that it was born at the dawn of the Reformation, and grew with its growth.
control.work: The State in Its Relations with the Church (1838; 3rd ed., 1839 text)
control.locator: Chapter V (running head; on toleration and private judgment), the origin of the doctrine of private judgment

notes: Early text is the archive.org OCR djvu of the Princeton copy of the 3rd edition (title page 'Third edition, MDCCCXXXIX'); Gladstone says three editions appeared without textual change, so the 1838 wording is the same. OCR leaves double spaces and spaced punctuation (': namely', '" dutiful necessity,"') which are verbatim in the file; the span covers Chapters I-VIII (Gladstone's own text, from 'CHAPTER I.' to 'THE END.') but includes his footnotes and some OCR noise. Later work is Gutenberg #47862 (clean); the span includes Macaulay's 1839 letters, which Gladstone quotes inside his text, and the Hansard extract, plus his footnotes. The announced passage states both the old and the new view ('My opinion ... now is the direct opposite of what it was then'). The early passage states the general principle (governments 'cognizant of religious truth and falsehood, and bound to the maintenance and propagation of the former'); the book applies it to the Irish Church, and the 1868 text itself summarizes the book that way. The unannounced passage states the new view as an argument for disestablishment on civil justice, with only 'now' as a time marker. Wikipedia (Gladstone): 'His book The State in its Relations with the Church argued that England had neglected its great duty to the Church of England ... In 1868 the Irish Church Resolutions were proposed ... disestablishment of the Church of Ireland'; the Chapter of Autobiography is listed in its bibliography.
